Multilevel latent profile analysis

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/lpa.Rmd
lpa.Rmd

Latent profile analysis (LPA) is a person-centred statistical approach used to identify unobserved subpopulations within a heterogeneous population. It assumes that the observed data arise from a finite mixture of latent profiles, each characterized by a distinct pattern of means across a set of continuous indicators. Rather than assuming that all observations originate from a single homogeneous population, LPA allows individuals to differ in their underlying response patterns and estimates the number and characteristics of the latent profiles, their relative proportions, and the posterior probability of each observation belonging to each profile. From a statistical perspective, LPA is a finite Gaussian mixture model in which the observed distribution is represented as a weighted combination of profile-specific multivariate normal distributions (Scrucca et al., 2024).

Conventional LPA assumes that observations are independent of one another. This assumption may be inappropriate when the data have a hierarchical structure, in which observations are nested within higher-level units. For example, courses completed by the same students or employees belonging to the same departments may exhibit similarities arising from their shared context. Such dependencies may also result in differences in the distribution of latent profiles across groups. Multilevel latent profile analysis extends the conventional model by accounting for heterogeneity at both the individual and group levels (Vermunt, 2003; Asparouhov & Muthén, 2008; Mäkikangas et al., 2018).

In multilevel LPA, individuals are classified into latent profiles based on their patterns across the observed indicators, while groups are classified into latent group classes according to the distribution of individual-level profiles within them. Consequently, the model captures not only differences between individuals but also systematic differences in the composition of groups. For example, two groups may contain individuals belonging to the same set of latent profiles but differ in the relative proportions of individuals assigned to each profile. These differences are represented through group-specific profile probabilities.

Formally, let CijC_{ij} denote the latent profile membership of observation ii in group jj, and let GjG_j denote the latent group class of group jj. The composition of each group class is described by the conditional profile probabilities:

πk∣m=P(Cij=k∣Gj=m),∑kπk∣m=1. \pi_{k\mid m}=P(C_{ij}=k\mid G_j=m), \qquad \sum_k\pi_{k\mid m}=1.

Here, πk∣m\pi_{k\mid m} represents the probability that an observation belongs to individual-level profile kk, conditional on its group belonging to group class mm. These probabilities therefore characterize the distribution of individual-level profiles within each group class. Groups assigned to different group classes may consequently differ in their profile composition, even when the underlying individual-level profiles are identical.

An important feature of this specification is that the profile-specific means and variances are assumed to remain invariant across group classes. In other words, the individual-level profiles retain the same measurement characteristics regardless of the group class in which they occur. Differences between group classes are therefore expressed through the relative prevalence of individual-level profiles rather than through changes in the profiles’ underlying definitions. This constraint provides a common measurement structure for comparing group classes and facilitates the interpretation of differences in their profile compositions.

Houle et al. (2026) provide an overview of multilevel latent profile analysis and its extensions, including alternative specifications that allow additional sources of heterogeneity at the individual and group levels. In the latents package, the function multilpa() estimates the multilevel latent profile model using maximum likelihood estimation and the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977). The algorithm alternates between estimating posterior probabilities of latent class membership and updating the model parameters until convergence is reached.

The analysis below proceeds in the usual order: the extent of nesting, a first model, a check of its assumptions, the numbers of profiles and group classes, interpretation and evaluation of the chosen model, and the relation of its classes to another variable.

Data

course_engagement contains 1,422 course enrolments of 106 students.

  • Group: student.
  • Indicators: five activity measures (browse, lectures, forum_read, forum_post, attendance), standardized within course (0 is the course mean, 1 one standard deviation above it).
  • External variable: previous_grade, the standardized grade of the preceding course.

Two further columns hold the generating structure, engagement for each enrolment and student_type for each student; they serve only to check recovery.

library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")

Clustering within groups

descriptives() summarizes the indicators and their intraclass correlation (icc), the share of variance between groups, estimated from the one-way analysis of variance (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979).

descriptives(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student")
#>     variable    n n_missing      mean    sd   min  max n_distinct n_groups sd_within sd_between
#> 1     browse 1422         0 -2.81e-05 0.989 -3.14 2.49        398      106     0.890      0.502
#> 2   lectures 1422         0 -4.22e-05 0.989 -2.91 3.22        399      106     0.945      0.392
#> 3 forum_read 1422         0  7.03e-05 0.989 -2.73 2.81        400      106     0.872      0.524
#> 4 forum_post 1422         0 -2.11e-05 0.989 -2.61 3.10        397      106     0.912      0.458
#> 5 attendance 1422         0  7.74e-05 0.989 -2.45 2.41        401      106     0.873      0.525
#>      icc
#> 1 0.1923
#> 2 0.0878
#> 3 0.2240
#> 4 0.1503
#> 5 0.2215

Between 9% (lectures) and 22% (forum_read, attendance) of the variance lies between students. Enrolments of one student are therefore not independent, and the students are the independent units of the analysis. Most of the variance remains within students, where the profiles operate.

A first model

n_profiles and n_group_classes set the numbers of profiles and group classes; n_starts sets the number of EM starts, seed makes them reproducible and cores runs them in parallel. The default covariance structure is "VVI" (Celeux & Govaert, 1995): profile-specific variances and no covariances within profiles, so the indicators are independent given the profile.

fit <- multilpa(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
fit
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 2 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Log likelihood: -8439.816424 | AIC: 16925.633 | BIC (groups): 16986.892
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 9 | best log likelihood reached by 10 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.3715 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 587.9; weight effective n: 606.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 58.7% (834)   profile_2 41.3% (588)
#> Group classes group_class_1 32.5% (34)   group_class_2 67.5% (72)
#> 
#> Means
#>   indicator profile_1 profile_2
#>      browse     0.540    -0.766
#>    lectures     0.427    -0.606
#>  forum_read     0.620    -0.879
#>  forum_post     0.530    -0.753
#>  attendance     0.649    -0.921
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

Profile 1 (58.7% of the enrolments) lies 0.43 to 0.65 standard deviations above the course mean on all indicators and profile 2 (41.3%) 0.61 to 0.92 below it: engaged and disengaged enrolments. The BIC uses the 106 students as its sample size. All ten starts reached the same log likelihood.

Checking local independence

Under a diagonal structure, any association between indicators within a profile can only be represented by additional profiles, which then describe the association rather than types of observations. The "residuals" table compares each within-profile association with the value the model implies, with p-values adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

head(get_results(fit, "residuals"), 6)
#>     profile indicator_1 indicator_2     kind observed expected residual effective_n statistic df
#> 1 profile_1    lectures  attendance gaussian    0.234        0    0.234         834      6.87 NA
#> 2 profile_2  forum_read  attendance gaussian    0.229        0    0.229         588      5.63 NA
#> 3 profile_1  forum_read  attendance gaussian    0.209        0    0.209         834      6.11 NA
#> 4 profile_1  forum_post  attendance gaussian    0.203        0    0.203         834      5.94 NA
#> 5 profile_2      browse  attendance gaussian    0.192        0    0.192         588      4.71 NA
#> 6 profile_1      browse  attendance gaussian    0.173        0    0.173         834      5.04 NA
#>    p_value p_adjusted
#> 1 6.37e-12   1.27e-10
#> 2 1.80e-08   8.99e-08
#> 3 1.00e-09   1.00e-08
#> 4 2.87e-09   1.91e-08
#> 5 2.43e-06   8.10e-06
#> 6 4.62e-07   1.85e-06

The six largest residuals all involve attendance, in both profiles: its within-profile correlations with the other measures are 0.17 to 0.23, with adjusted p-values below 0.00001. The data documentation confirms the source: attendance is generated from the four click measures (?course_engagement). covariance_model = "full" estimates all within-profile covariances ("VVV"); local_dependence frees selected pairs.

full <- multilpa(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                 n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                 covariance_model = "full", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
compare_models(diagonal = fit, full = full)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model     Profiles  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC    ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> --------  --------  -------------  --  --------  --------  ------  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> diagonal         2              2  23  -8439.82  16986.89  160.14   0.000  17175.69     0.94       0.98      0           0.94             0.97
#> full             2              2  43  -8313.11  16826.75    0.00   1.000  17128.35     0.91       0.97      0           0.94             0.97

The full structure adds 20 parameters and lowers the BIC by 160 (BIC weight 1.000). The profiles and group classes retain their sizes and meaning; the numbers of classes are chosen under this structure.

Choosing the numbers of profiles and group classes

enumerate_classes() fits every combination of the requested numbers of profiles and group classes and returns information criteria, classification statistics and estimation checks. For the group classes, Lukočienė et al. (2010) recommend the BIC (Schwarz, 1978) with the number of groups as sample size (bic_groups). Group classes require at least two profiles, so candidates with one profile and several group classes fail by design.

grid <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                          covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 1:3,
                          n_group_classes = 1:4, n_starts = 5, seed = 1)

get_deltas() gives the improvement of each criterion when a profile or a group class is added.

subset(get_deltas(grid), criterion == "bic_groups")
#>            candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model  criterion value delta_profile

#> 2  profiles2_groups1          2               1   VVV bic_groups 17170         343.1

#> 12 profiles2_groups4             12.06 profiles3_groups3

Two profiles are supported unambiguously: the second profile lowers the BIC by 343, and a third raises it at every number of group classes, by 55 to 67. For the group classes, the second lowers the BIC by 344, the third by 26 and the fourth by 3, while group-level separation declines (relative entropy 0.942, 0.816 and 0.797; lowest group average posterior 0.971, 0.903 and 0.830). The AWE (Banfield & Raftery, 1993) and the ICL computed on the enrolments (Biernacki et al., 2000), which penalize uncertain classification, select two group classes (get_best(grid)). The model with two profiles and two group classes is retained. The small gains of further group classes have an identifiable source: engagement changes along each student’s course sequence, a dependence that multilevel LPA does not model and that additional group classes partly absorb; lta() models the sequence directly (see the latent transition analysis article).

Two candidates with three profiles (two and four group classes) raise warnings: one profile has too little membership for its 20 free means and covariances, and both reached their best likelihood from a single start. The AIC, whose penalty is the weakest, favours three profiles with four group classes; the BIC rejects three profiles at every number of group classes, so the warnings do not affect the choice by BIC.

The chosen model

Profile 1 (59.0%) lies 0.42 to 0.63 standard deviations above the course mean and profile 2 (41.0%) 0.61 to 0.91 below it; attendance and forum reading separate the profiles most, lecture viewing least. get_results() returns the means and variances, get_results(full, "covariances") the covariances.

get_results(full)

All variances are below 1, the variance of the standardized indicators: enrolments within a profile are more homogeneous than the sample. The profile plot shows the means, with the profile shares in the labels.

plot_profiles(full)

Group classes

The "profile_probabilities" table gives πk∣m\pi_{k \mid m} (probability) and the proportion of groups in each class (group_class_probability).

get_results(full, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1       0.164                   0.325
#> 2           1       2       0.836                   0.325
#> 3           2       1       0.793                   0.675
#> 4           2       2       0.207                   0.675

Group class 2 (67.5% of the students) has 79.3% engaged enrolments and group class 1 (32.5%) 16.4%: mostly engaged and mostly disengaged students. Neither class is pure: a mostly engaged student is disengaged in about one course in five, a mostly disengaged student engaged in about one in six. Students are mixtures of profiles in class-specific proportions. The prevalence plot shows these probabilities.

plot_prevalence(full)

Class sizes and classification

effective_count sums the posterior probabilities and is therefore not necessarily an integer.

get_results(full, "counts")
#>         level class effective_count effective_proportion
#> 1 individuals     1           838.8                0.590
#> 2 individuals     2           583.2                0.410
#> 3      groups     1            34.5                0.325
#> 4      groups     2            71.5                0.675

The profiles hold 838.8 and 583.2 enrolments, the group classes 34.5 and 71.5 students; no class is small enough to threaten estimation. Relative entropy measures the separation of the classes on a scale from 0 (no separation) to 1 (certain assignment) (Ramaswamy et al., 1993); it is not a measure of fit.

get_results(full, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         2    1422       92.36            0.906
#> 2      groups         2     106        4.25            0.942

Relative entropy is 0.906 for the enrolments and 0.942 for the students. The average posterior probability of the assigned class gives the same information by class.

get_results(full, "average_posteriors")
#>         level assigned_class class n_assigned average_posterior
#> 1 individuals              1     1        842           0.97775
#> 2 individuals              1     2        842           0.02225
#> 3 individuals              2     1        580           0.02674
#> 4 individuals              2     2        580           0.97326
#> 5      groups              1     1         35           0.97087
#> 6      groups              1     2         35           0.02913
#> 7      groups              2     1         71           0.00698
#> 8      groups              2     2         71           0.99302

The average posteriors are 0.978 and 0.973 for the profiles and 0.971 and 0.993 for the group classes. Assignments are therefore accurate at both levels, although analyses of assigned classes still ignore the remaining uncertainty; the three-step methods below account for it. The "assignments" table adds the most probable profile and group_class, the uncertainty of the profile assignment and the posterior probabilities to the data.

get_results(full, "assignments", data = course_engagement) |> head()
#>   student course sequence browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance previous_grade

The first student’s first two enrolments are assigned to the engaged profile, the second with an uncertainty of 0.148, and the next four to the disengaged profile with uncertainties below 0.001; the student belongs to the mostly disengaged group class.

Recovery of the known structure

The truth argument cross-tabulates the assignments with the generating labels; class numbers are arbitrary, so correspondence is read from the table.

get_results(full, "assignments", data = course_engagement,
            truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
#>    assignment class        truth      value   n proportion
#> 1     profile     1   engagement disengaged  18     0.0308
#> 2     profile     2   engagement disengaged 567     0.9692
#> 3     profile     1   engagement    engaged 824     0.9845
#> 4     profile     2   engagement    engaged  13     0.0155
#> 5 group_class     1 student_type  committed   1     0.0161
#> 6 group_class     2 student_type  committed  61     0.9839
#> 7 group_class     1 student_type   wavering  34     0.7727
#> 8 group_class     2 student_type   wavering  10     0.2273

Profile 1 contains 824 of the 837 engaged enrolments and profile 2 567 of the 585 disengaged ones (98% and 97%). Group class 2 contains 61 of the 62 committed students but also 10 of the 44 wavering ones. The model classifies the students with high certainty (relative entropy 0.942), yet recovers the wavering students less well: group classes differ only in their proportions of profiles, so a wavering student whose enrolments happen to be mostly engaged resembles a committed one.

Uncertainty of the estimates

parameter_inference() returns each estimate with its standard error and 95% Wald interval, from the observed information by default; vcov_type = "robust" gives sandwich standard errors with the students as clusters. The first ten rows are the profile means.

inference <- parameter_inference(full)
head(inference, 10)
#>          level   outcome       term parameter estimate standard_error statistic   p_value
#> 1  measurement profile_1     browse      mean    0.531         0.0280      18.9  4.52e-80
#> 2  measurement profile_1   lectures      mean    0.422         0.0331      12.8  3.07e-37

#> 4  measurement profile_1 forum_post      mean    0.527         0.0306      17.2  1.87e-66
#> 5  measurement profile_1 attendance      mean    0.632         0.0240      26.3 4.39e-152
#> 6  measurement profile_2     browse      mean   -0.764         0.0328     -23.3 6.90e-120
#> 7  measurement profile_2   lectures      mean   -0.607         0.0320     -19.0  3.96e-80
#> 8  measurement profile_2 forum_read      mean   -0.881         0.0276     -31.9 5.69e-223
#> 9  measurement profile_2 forum_post      mean   -0.758         0.0286     -26.5 5.45e-155
#> 10 measurement profile_2 attendance      mean   -0.908         0.0287     -31.7 5.51e-220
#>    p_adjusted conf_low conf_high
#> 1    4.52e-80    0.476     0.586
#> 2    3.07e-37    0.357     0.487
#> 3   1.38e-123    0.562     0.664
#> 4    1.87e-66    0.467     0.587
#> 5   4.39e-152    0.585     0.679
#> 6   6.90e-120   -0.829    -0.700
#> 7    3.96e-80   -0.670    -0.544
#> 8   5.69e-223   -0.935    -0.827
#> 9   5.45e-155   -0.814    -0.702
#> 10  5.51e-220   -0.964    -0.852

The standard errors of the means are 0.024 to 0.033, and the intervals of the two profiles are far apart. The last six rows contain the group-level probabilities.

tail(inference, 6)
#>      level       outcome          term   parameter estimate standard_error statistic p_value
#> 41 profile     profile_1 group_class_1 probability    0.164         0.0224        NA      NA
#> 42 profile     profile_2 group_class_1 probability    0.836         0.0224        NA      NA
#> 43 profile     profile_1 group_class_2 probability    0.793         0.0161        NA      NA
#> 44 profile     profile_2 group_class_2 probability    0.207         0.0161        NA      NA
#> 45   group group_class_1          <NA> probability    0.325         0.0475        NA      NA
#> 46   group group_class_2          <NA> probability    0.675         0.0475        NA      NA
#>    p_adjusted conf_low conf_high
#> 41         NA    0.125     0.213
#> 42         NA    0.787     0.875
#> 43         NA    0.760     0.823
#> 44         NA    0.177     0.240
#> 45         NA    0.240     0.424
#> 46         NA    0.576     0.760

The group level is estimated less precisely. The share of mostly disengaged students is 0.325 (95% interval 0.240 to 0.424); the probability of an engaged enrolment is 0.164 (0.125 to 0.213) in that class and 0.793 (0.760 to 0.823) in the other.

Stability across seeds

sensitivity() refits the model from several seeds and compares the maxima and classifications.

sensitivity(full, seeds = 1:5)
#>   seed log_likelihood converged iterations optimum best agreement
#> 1    1          -8313      TRUE         12       1 TRUE         1
#> 2    2          -8313      TRUE         12       1 TRUE         1
#> 3    3          -8313      TRUE         12       1 TRUE         1
#> 4    4          -8313      TRUE         12       1 TRUE         1
#> 5    5          -8313      TRUE         12       1 TRUE         1

All five refits reach the log likelihood of -8313 with identical classifications (agreement of 1).

Relating the classes to other variables

Entering an external variable in the model can change the classes it is meant to explain. Three-step methods hold the classes fixed and correct for classification error (Bolck et al., 2004; Vermunt, 2010). r3step() regresses profile membership on predictors, with the last profile, here the disengaged one, as reference.

r3step(full, data = course_engagement, covariates = "previous_grade")
#>         level   outcome           term estimate standard_error statistic  p_value p_adjusted
#> 1 individuals profile_1    (Intercept)    0.394         0.1362      2.89 3.80e-03         NA
#> 2 individuals profile_1 previous_grade    0.615         0.0612     10.05 9.55e-24   9.55e-24
#>   conf_low conf_high
#> 1    0.127     0.661
#> 2    0.495     0.735

A previous grade one standard deviation higher increases the log odds of an engaged enrolment by 0.615 (95% interval 0.495 to 0.735), an odds ratio of about 1.85. three_step() compares the mean of a variable across profiles.

three_step(full, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade",
           contrast = "pairs")
#> Distal outcome: class differences (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class  vs  Difference          95% CI      p  p (BH)
#> -----  --  ----------  --------------  -----  ------
#>     2   1       -0.57  [-0.67, -0.47]  <.001   <.001

Previous grades are 0.57 standard deviations lower before disengaged than before engaged enrolments (95% interval 0.47 to 0.67). Both results are associations; temporal order alone does not establish an effect of grades on engagement. One-step alternatives enter predictors in the model (profile_covariates for observations, group_covariates for groups); fit_staged() holds the profiles fixed while the group classes are estimated. The covariates and case study articles compare these approaches.

Sampling weights

weights names a column of sampling weights, constant within the independent unit (here student). Estimation maximizes a weighted pseudo-log-likelihood, with weights normalized to sum to the number of students, and reports Kish’s (1965) effective sample size. The example doubles the weight of the simulated wavering students, as for a design that sampled them at half the rate, and uses the diagonal structure of the first model.

weighted_data <- transform(course_engagement,
                           survey_weight = ifelse(student_type == "wavering", 2, 1))
weighted_fit <- multilpa(weighted_data, vars = vars, id = "student",
                         n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                         weights = "survey_weight", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
weighted_fit
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 2 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Sampling weights `survey_weight` (pseudo maximum likelihood): Kish effective n 94.5 of 106 units
#> Log likelihood: -8341.125778 | AIC: 16728.252 | BIC (groups): 16789.511
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 9 | best log likelihood reached by 10 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.3759 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 714.8; weight effective n: 563.8.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 49.5% (701)   profile_2 50.5% (715)
#> Group classes group_class_1 45.2% (48)   group_class_2 54.8% (58)
#> 
#> Means
#>   indicator profile_1 profile_2
#>      browse     0.525    -0.770
#>    lectures     0.446    -0.608
#>  forum_read     0.605    -0.877
#>  forum_post     0.515    -0.742
#>  attendance     0.655    -0.921
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

Weighting changes the prevalence of the classes, not their definition: the mostly disengaged group class grows from 32.5% to 45.2% of the students and the engaged profile shrinks from 58.7% to 49.5% of the enrolments, while the profile means barely change (browsing in the engaged profile 0.525 against 0.540). The effective sample size is 94.5 of 106 students.

For weighted fits, parameter_inference() uses sandwich standard errors by default; vcov_type = "observed" is not available, because inverse-information standard errors do not represent the sampling variance under unequal weights.

head(parameter_inference(weighted_fit), 4)
#>         level   outcome       term parameter estimate standard_error statistic   p_value p_adjusted
#> 1 measurement profile_1     browse      mean    0.525         0.0324      16.2  6.16e-59   6.16e-59
#> 2 measurement profile_1   lectures      mean    0.446         0.0367      12.2  4.54e-34   4.54e-34
#> 3 measurement profile_1 forum_read      mean    0.605         0.0264      22.9 8.01e-116  8.01e-116
#> 4 measurement profile_1 forum_post      mean    0.515         0.0319      16.2  9.48e-59   9.48e-59
#>   conf_low conf_high
#> 1    0.462     0.589
#> 2    0.374     0.518
#> 3    0.553     0.657
#> 4    0.453     0.578

weights is also available in lta(), mixture_regression() and the other model families of multilpa(). The parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test does not accept weighted fits, because its simulations do not reproduce a sampling design.

Other options of multilpa()

  • Covariance structures. model takes the fourteen mclust codes ("EII" to "VVV"); volume, shape and orientation set the components separately; local_dependence frees selected pairs.
  • Missing values. missing = "fiml" uses all observed indicators of incomplete rows.
  • Indicator types. categorical, ordinal and count combine categorical, ordinal and count indicators with continuous ones (see the latent class analysis vignette).
  • Model families. family fits group-class models from raw ratings ("additive", "dispersion", "additive_dispersion", "restricted_cross_level", "full_cross_level"; see the group-class and cross-level article).
  • Order of observations. time orders each group’s observations for the sequence tables and plot_sequences(); lta() models transitions between profiles.
  • Centring. centering = "person" subtracts each group’s mean, so that profiles describe deviations from a group’s usual level and group classes describe patterns of change; "grand" subtracts the sample mean.

Other tables, plots and functions

The calls below list the other tables, functions and views available for a fitted model. Each comment states what the call returns.

# Tables: get_results(full, what)
get_results(full, "all")                          # every table, as a named list
get_results(full, "covariances")                  # within-profile residual covariances
get_results(full, "posteriors")                   # one row per observation and profile
get_results(full, "posteriors", format = "wide")  # one row per observation
get_results(full, "group_posteriors")             # one row per group and group class
get_results(full, "classification")               # class sizes and average posteriors
get_results(full, "average_posteriors")           # mean posterior by assigned class
get_results(full, "classification_errors")        # P(assigned class | true class)
get_results(full, "bch_weights")                  # weights for three-step analysis
get_results(full, "residuals")                    # residual correlations within profiles
get_results(full, "information_criteria")         # AIC, BIC and the other criteria
get_results(full, "model")                        # one row describing the fit
get_results(full, "data")                         # the variables used in the fit
as.data.frame(full)                               # the profile table

# Summaries and diagnostics
descriptives(full)                    # indicator summaries with the ICC
descriptives(full, by = "profile")    # the same, by assigned profile
diagnostics(full)                     # every classification diagnostic
report(full)                          # summary, diagnostics and plots together

# Inference and likelihood
parameter_inference(full)             # standard errors and Wald intervals
confint(full)                         # confidence intervals
vcov(full)                            # covariance matrix of the estimates
logLik(full)                          # log likelihood
AIC(full)                             # Akaike information criterion
BIC(full)                             # BIC with the number of groups
nobs(full)                            # number of groups

# Plots: the plot_ functions, each with what = and "all"
plot_views()                                   # every view and what it shows
plot_profiles(full, what = "bars")              # profile means with 95% intervals
plot_profiles(full, what = "heatmap")           # means in standard deviations
plot_profiles(full, what = "all")               # every profile view
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "sizes")          # effective size of each profile
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "entropy")        # per-case classification uncertainty
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "posteriors")     # posterior of each assigned profile
plot_diagnostics(full, what = "avepp")          # average posteriors, assigned by posterior class
plot(full, what = "all")                        # every view this fit supports

# Other functions
sensitivity(full, seeds = 1:10)       # refits under several seeds

The class enumeration article covers enumerate_classes() and get_candidate(); the latent transition analysis article covers lta(), get_tna() and get_group_tna(). The evaluation article on the package website covers bootstrap_lrt(), and the covariates article covers three_step(), r3step() and fit_staged().

Assumptions

  • Profiles have the same means and covariances in every group class.
  • Observations are independent given the class of their group, and groups are independent. Observations ordered in time, such as a student’s course sequence, can violate the first condition; lta() models the order.
  • Under the default diagonal structure, indicators are independent within a profile; covariance_model = "full", model and local_dependence relax this, and the "residuals" table checks it.
  • The numbers of profiles and group classes are chosen from the criteria (see the class enumeration and model selection articles).

Reporting

A report of a multilevel LPA states:

  • the indicators, their scaling, the grouping variable and the intraclass correlations;
  • the covariance structure and the evidence for it;
  • the candidates compared, the criteria used and the reasons for the chosen numbers of profiles and group classes;
  • the number of starts, the replication of the best log likelihood and the seeds;
  • the profile means with standard errors or intervals, the profile probabilities of each group class and the class sizes at both levels;
  • relative entropy and average posterior probabilities at both levels;
  • for external variables, the method (three-step, BCH or one-step) and its estimates with intervals.
